summary: handle() now rate-limits every API key with an in-memory token bucket: 60 requests a minute, then a 429 with a Retry-After header.

questions.question: What does a client get once its API key has used up its requests for the minute?
questions.rubric: A 429 response with a Retry-After header computed from the bucket refill; the route is not called.

rules.feedback: Right: a 429 with Retry-After, and the route never runs.
Which error? A 429 with a Retry-After header.

default.feedback: Missed: the client gets a 429 with Retry-After.

questions.question: Why limit per API key rather than one global limit for the whole service?
questions.rubric: One heavy tenant was starving the others; a global limit would punish everyone for one key's traffic.

rules.feedback: Yes: per key isolates the noisy tenant instead of throttling everyone.
Yes: per key isolates the noisy tenant instead of throttling everyone.

default.feedback: Missed: a global limit punishes every customer for one key's traffic.

questions.question: The API runs on two app servers behind a load balancer. What limit does one key really get?
questions.rubric: Up to twice the limit: each process keeps its own _buckets dict, so the limit is per server until the state moves to a shared store.

rules.feedback: Exactly: each server has its own bucket, so the real limit doubles.
Exactly: each server has its own bucket, so the real limit doubles.
Not 60: each server keeps its own bucket, so it is up to 120.

default.feedback: Missed: the buckets live in process memory, one per server.

questions.question: Which existing clients does this change put at risk, and how?
questions.rubric: Clients that retry immediately without honouring Retry-After will loop on 429s and add load; the mobile app's retry logic needs a backoff first.

rules.feedback: Right: clients that ignore Retry-After will hammer the API harder.
Close: the risk is clients that retry without reading Retry-After.

default.feedback: Missed: aggressive retry loops turn 429s into more load.

questions.question: How would you show in a test that the limit actually triggers?
questions.rubric: Send 61 requests for one key inside a minute (or with a fake clock) and assert the 61st is a 429 with Retry-After, and that another key is unaffected.

rules.feedback: Good: the 61st request is the one that must come back 429.
Good; pin the boundary: request 61 is the first 429.

default.feedback: Missed: drive one key past 60 requests and assert the 429.

verdicts.text: You know what this limiter does and exactly where it will bite in production.
Solid grasp; re-read the parts flagged above before it ships.
Re-read the diff: the limiter's scope and its failure modes are not clear yet.
